opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to what you're optimizing for. A PhD trains you to be a researcher in the academic sense: you pick a narrow problem, you spend years on it, you write papers, you learn how to convince reviewers. That's a valuable skill set, but if your goal is to go into industry, especially into a place doing large-scale AI work, a lot of what actually matters is different. It's engineering ability, being able to build systems that work at scale, debugging, moving fast, collaborating with a team toward a shared goal rather than toward your own first-author paper.

In my own experience, the things that made me useful weren't the number of publications. Tianshou, for example, was an open-source project, and EnvPool was about making environment simulation really fast. That's engineering work, and it ended up having more impact, and getting me more attention from industry, than a typical paper would. When I joined OpenAI, nobody really cared whether I had a PhD. They cared whether I could make the infrastructure work and help train the models.

There's also the opportunity cost. Five or six years is a long time, especially in a field moving this fast. If you spend those years in industry, you're working with far more compute, much stronger colleagues on real problems, and you get feedback from reality instead of from reviewers. You can grow much faster that way.

I'm not saying a PhD is useless. If you love research for its own sake, or you want to become a professor, it makes total sense. But if you already know you want to end up in industry, I'd say just go. Build things, show what you can do, and let your work speak for itself. The credential matters much less than people think.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should be careful here, because I'm not saying a PhD is useless. I'm saying that if you already know you want to go into industry, especially something like applied machine learning or infrastructure, a PhD is often not the shortest path, and sometimes it's not even a better path.

The reason is pretty simple. What industry actually values is the ability to build things that work, to debug, to ship, to collaborate with other engineers. A lot of that you learn by doing. When I was working on Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, most of what I learned came from users opening issues, from reading other people's code, from trying to make something reliable rather than novel. That's a very different skill set from what a PhD is optimized for, which is going deep on one narrow question and producing papers.

And a PhD is expensive. Not just the money, but five or six years of your life during which you could be gaining real experience, building a track record, and honestly getting paid reasonably well. By the time you graduate, the field has moved. In machine learning especially, the thing you spent three years on might be solved or irrelevant.

There's also a kind of myth that you need the credential to get in the door. For research scientist roles at some labs, sure, it still matters. But for the majority of engineering and applied roles, people care about what you've actually done. If you have an open-source project that people use, or you've contributed to something meaningful, that speaks louder than a line on a CV.

So my view is: do a PhD if you genuinely love research, if you want to be in academia, or if the specific role you want truly requires it. But don't do it as a default, or because you think it's the safe choice. For most people heading into industry, it isn't necessary, and the opportunity cost is real.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say a PhD is unnecessary for everyone. It depends on what you want to do in industry. If you want to work in research, a PhD can be valuable, and some roles require it. But if your goal is to build products or work as an engineer, you can often learn more directly by doing the job. You’re gaining practical experience, learning how to work with a team, and understanding what users actually need.

A PhD is a substantial investment of time, so I think it makes sense if you enjoy research itself. If you’re doing it only because you think it’s the next credential you need to enter industry, it’s worth asking whether working in industry would be a more direct path.
